analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan with prices negotiated directly from drugmakers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by just two Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicare to offer its own prescription drug plan nationwide and make it the default plan for anyone in Medicare's Part D drug program unless they pick another one. It would lift the current legal ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices for that plan, using prices in peer countries like Canada and Germany as a benchmark, and steer patients toward cheaper equivalent drugs when medically appropriate. It would also bar former drug-company lobbyists and senior executives of drug companies under federal enforcement from serving on the advisory committee that guides pricing.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries in the Part D drug program would gain a government-run plan whose drug prices are actively negotiated instead of set by private-market bargaining, with a uniform premium nationwide and an easier appeals process if a drug is denied. The government plan would be the default, so beneficiaries would get it automatically rather than having to shop among dozens of private plans. Taxpayers and beneficiaries alike would bear less of the cost of high drug prices if negotiation brought prices down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries in the Part D drug program

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare to run at least one prescription drug plan serving the entire country, and makes it the default plan for all Part D enrollees unless they choose a different plan — so every beneficiary is covered by the negotiated-price plan unless they opt out.

Lifts the current legal ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices: CMS would have to negotiate purchase prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers for drugs in the Medicare-operated plan, and encourage use of more affordable therapeutic equivalents where medically appropriate.

Bases price negotiations on real-world benchmarks: the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality would assess each drug's clinical benefit using the median retail prices in peer countries (Canada, the UK, France, Japan, Australia, Germany), safety data, and comparative-effectiveness research, then recommend prices to start from.
Charges a single uniform premium nationwide, based on the plan's average actuarial cost, so beneficiaries would not face a patchwork of premiums that vary by state or insurer.

Adds a streamlined appeals process for denied drugs under the government plan, based on professional medical judgment, and creates an advisory committee to review price petitions that bars former drug-company lobbyists and former senior executives of drug companies operating under federal settlements or enforcement actions for six years.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the main cost: prices for drugs in the Medicare plan would be negotiated, potentially benchmarked to lower international prices, cutting into U.S. sales revenue — money the industry argues helps fund research into new drugs. Private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that sponsor Part D plans would also lose enrollment to the default government plan, and HHS would take on the cost of operating the new plan (financed through beneficiary premiums and Medicare payments).
analysis.who_pays_short: Drugmakers and private Part D plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: The government plan's negotiated prices would apply only to drugs covered under that one plan — beneficiaries who opt for a private Part D plan would not get the negotiated prices, so savings would not reach everyone automatically.

Because the government plan would be the default with a single uniform premium set by average cost, enrollment patterns could shift costs around: if healthier beneficiaries migrate to private plans or vice versa, the premium for those remaining in the public plan could rise, an adverse-selection risk the bill does not directly address.

Lower prices benchmarked to international list prices would mean less revenue for pharmaceutical manufacturers, and the industry's standard argument — that lower U.S. prices leave less money to invest in developing new medicines — is a real tradeoff that supporters of negotiation have to weigh against the savings to patients.

The bill would also eliminate fallback prescription drug plans after 2020, replacing that structure with the new Medicare-operated option, which adds transition complexity for plans and beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of people in Medicare's drug program, the upside is direct and large: a default plan whose prices are negotiated rather than accepted, benchmarked to what peer countries pay, with a uniform premium and a simpler appeals process. The costs fall mostly on drug manufacturers and private Part D plan sponsors rather than on taxpayers or patients, though the R&D-revenue tradeoff is real and the negotiated prices would only reach people enrolled in the government plan. On balance, the design is straightforward and the main weakness is its narrow scope — negotiation for one plan rather than the whole program.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Dick Durbin introduced the bill on October 21, 2019, joined by one cosponsor, Sen. Sherrod Brown; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The action history shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor consideration at any point.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill advancing, so it died in committee under the rule that unfinished bills lapse when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and the private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that sponsor Part D plans came out ahead: the existing ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices stayed in place and no public drug plan competed with their products.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drugmakers and private Part D insurers

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction — the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held on it.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it received no floor consideration at any point in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls ever occurred on the bill; both of its sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee, which held the bill, took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would end the legal ban on Medicare negotiating prices for drugs in the new government plan and benchmark starting prices to what peer countries pay, directly cutting into U.S. drug revenue. The industry's interest in preserving the negotiation ban runs against beneficiaries who pay the resulting prices.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: A nationally available, default Medicare-operated plan would draw enrollment away from privately sponsored drug plans, shrinking their customer base. Their current market position depends on the absence of a government-run competitor, which is what this bill would have created.
